what_it_does: Rowhammer is a hardware vulnerability in DRAM memory chips (the large, dense storage used as main memory in computers): repeatedly accessing one row of memory cells at high frequency causes neighboring rows to lose charge and flip their stored bits, potentially corrupting data or enabling an attacker to take control of a system. The DDR5 memory standard added Per-Row Activation Counters (PRAC) — tiny counters inside each DRAM chip that track how many times each row has been accessed — and mandate a corrective action when a counter gets too high. The problem is that updating these counters on every single memory access adds about 10% runtime overhead even for completely normal, harmless programs. MoPAC cuts this cost by updating counters only on a random sample of accesses (say, one in ten), while compensating by triggering the corrective action at a proportionally lower threshold (one-tenth as high), so the security guarantee is maintained while the average overhead drops dramatically. Two variants are proposed — one in the memory controller outside the DRAM chip, and one inside the DRAM chip itself. This is from the abstract only.
